en: Oṃ, homage to the glorious Kālacakra!
The Mother is of all forms and consists of the stainless emptiness.
And he is the all-pervading Lord, whose body is filled with the peaceful flavor of non-duality;
by means of which form he generates the noble lineage of the Victors.
Homage to him, whose peace is purified by innate yoga!
Having prostrated at the lotus feet of the glorious Guru for my own remembrance, [I shall explain] the ritual procedure for the worship of Kālacakra.
By his grace, this commentary on the *Sekoddeśa* is being written.

In this very place, at the glorious Dhānya Mahācaitya, the Blessed One, the illustrious Śākyasiṃha, being requested by those desiring to hear various tantras, taught the Mantramahāyāna. There, King Sucandra, whose body was a manifestation of Vajrapāṇi—the great Bodhisattva and lord of the ten stages—requested the Blessed One for the Paramādibuddha, the great tantra of twelve thousand [verses]. For it is thus stated in the prophecy of the Blessed One: "The site for awakening is the Great Awakening within the system of the Prajñāpāramitā;
the certain location for the Teacher is the great mountain Gṛdhrakūṭa."
The place proclaimed in the Mahāmantra system is the Śrīdharmadhātu,
[the abode] of the perfectly awakened ones of the three times, beginning with the Lokadhātu.

Whether it be the Vaibhāṣika, Sūtrānta, Dhāraṇī, Kalpa, or the teaching [of the Abhidharma], the Jina has not taught a single fixed position; rather, he did so out of consideration for the dispositions of sentient beings.
O Noble One, according to the diverse dispositions of sentient beings,
Maitreya will teach the method of the Perfection of Wisdom even on Vulture Peak,
while the Buddha will teach the pure method of Mantra at Śrīdhānya.

According to this statement, the Blessed One taught the Mantranaya only at Śrīdhānya. However, in other regions, for the sake of those people who were devoted to that tantra, another compiler—either a great Bodhisattva who is a lord of the ten stages or someone else—extensively composed the teaching of that particular tantra.
Sucandra said:
"Sucandra" means he is both beautiful (*śobhana*) and the moon (*candra*); it is because the moon of the *bodhicitta* has attained purity upon his head.
O Teacher, please explain to me in brief the sevenfold initiation, as well as the threefold and the unsurpassed [initiations], for the sake of attaining mundane and supramundane accomplishments. (1)

Regarding "the consecrations" (*seka*) and so forth: there are seven beginning with water; three beginning with the vase (*kumbha*); and the "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*), which is the fourth, the consecration of supramundane great wisdom-knowledge (*lokottara-mahāprajñājñāna*). This is for the sake of attaining both mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*). Among these, mundane accomplishment consists of sovereignty extending as far as the Akaniṣṭha realm through the meditation on the imagined maṇḍala-circle.

The supreme accomplishment (*uttarā siddhi*) consists in the attainment of the state of a Great Vajradhara, the Lord of the twelve stages, beginning from the first stage through the cultivation of a non-dual samādhi that is inseparable from compassion which does not take as its object the emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects in an undifferentiated manner. This is stated briefly by way of a summary.
The Blessed One said:
"The Blessed One" refers to one who possesses qualities such as sovereignty, or because he has shattered the four Māras.
Listen, Sucandra, to the supreme [instruction] regarding the purpose of the consecration, which is sevenfold and threefold;
I shall explain to you, by way of summary, the movement through the channels and the breath-control (āyāma).

Regarding "for the sake of initiation" (*sekārtham*): initiation (*seka*) and its purpose (*artha*) together constitute "for the sake of initiation. In this context, "initiation" refers to the ritual act of bestowing water and so forth; "purpose" refers to the objective of effecting the purification of the body and other aggregates. "The movement through the channels" (*nāḍīsaṃcāra*) refers to the six channels—lalanā, rasanā, avadhūtī, and those carrying feces, urine, and semen—which extend upward and downward.

The movement of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds; or else, the movement of the channels (*nāḍī*) according to their established positions. Furthermore, he will say right here: "This is the movement of the channels," and so forth. Regarding "expansion" (*āyāma*): it is the cessation of the movement of the wind within those very channels. From the root *yam*, meaning "to cease," with the prefix *pra* and the suffix *ghañ*. Here, expansion (*āyāma*) is the act of restraining, that is, cessation. And thus it is said in the *Ādibuddha*: "Prāṇāyāma is the stumbling of the two paths, as well as the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the middle. (LKCT 4.116b)

"Listen," and so forth: the entire meaning of the text is taught by means of the verses to be recited hereafter. To dispel the doubt as to how there can be a statement such as "I shall speak" based on a summary (*uddeśa*) in an explanatory tantra (*nirdeśatantra*), he first states that the summary (*uddeśa*) is threefold, beginning with the words "The summary is threefold," etc., in order to clearly demonstrate that the entire tantra—both concise and extensive—is purified by the six points beginning with the summary, after having separately defined the characteristics of these six, beginning with the summary and the exposition.
"The summary in the tantra is threefold; the exposition would likewise be threefold."
The summary, the great summary, and another, the detailed exposition. || 3 ||
The brief statement itself is the detailed exposition; this is called the recitation of the Tantra.
Furthermore, the sub-statement is the detailed exposition, which is the commentary (*pañjikā*) that analyzes the words (*padabhañjikā*). (4)
The Mahoddeśa, the Nirdesa, and the Tīkā which indicates all meanings—
these must be composed by those who have attained the superknowledges (abhijñā), and certainly not by mere scholars.

In that regard, "furthermore" (*apara*) refers to the *Mahānirdeśa*. Now, he states the enumeration of the summary (*uddeśa*) and so forth, beginning with "the summary itself," and so on. Therein, the summary itself is the detailed exposition (*nirdeśa*), which is the "recitation of the tantra" (*tantra-saṃgīti*). This is the correct chanting (*gīti*) by Bodhisattvas and others of the Yoga and Yoginī Tantras as manifested by the Blessed One. That is twofold, according to the distinction between summary and detailed exposition.

In this regard, just as from the *Paramādibuddha-mūlatantra* consisting of twelve thousand [verses], there is the compendium (*saṃgāna*) of the *Kālacakra-laghutantrarāja* of one thousand three hundred [verses] which was extensively extracted by the Blessed One—this being the compendium of the summary (*uddeśa-saṃgīti*)—and the compendium of the twelve-thousand-verse *Mūlatantra* which is the compendium of the detailed exposition (*nirdeśa-saṃgīti*); so too, for the *Samāja*, *Hevajra*, *Saṃvara*, and others, the distinction between the teaching of the concise and extensive tantras should be understood as the compendium of the summary and the compendium of the detailed exposition.

Because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "the summary and the exposition" (*pratyuddeśaś ca nirdeśa*), the word *prati* is also applied to the exposition (*nirdeśa*). Because of the word "and" in the phrase "the great summary and the exposition" (*mahoddeśaś ca nirdeśa*), the word *mahat* is also applied to the exposition. Regarding the phrase "by those who have attained the superknowledges" (*abhijñālābhibhiḥ*), this refers specifically to the great Bodhisattvas who are masters of the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvara*). Regarding the word "that" (*sā*), the compendium (*saṃgīti*) is twofold, as are the word-commentary (*pañjikā*) and the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*). Regarding the word "by the scholars" (*paṇḍitaiḥ*), this refers to those who have not yet attained the [Bodhisattva] stages. Now, with the two verses beginning with "In this way" (*evam*), he explains the entry into the tantra. Thus, it is purified by the six parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) and by the fourfold Vajra-yogas.
By means of the four types of enlightenment, and through the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and the six families. || 6 ||
The *Ādibuddha*, designated as *Kālacakra*, consists of five pure chapters concerning the world-system and other subjects, and is established by means of the two truths. (7)
First is the sevenfold initiation, which is the means of entry for the ignorant;
it is threefold according to worldly convention, while the fourth is from the perspective of ultimate truth.
My teaching of phenomena as a Vajra-holder is by means of the two truths:
the conventional truth of the world and the ultimate truth. (9)

In this context, "by means of the six points" refers to the summary (uddeśa), the counter-summary (pratyuddeśa), the great summary (mahoddeśa), the detailed exposition (nirdeśa), the counter-exposition (pratinirdeśa), and the great exposition (mahānirdeśa). "By means of the fourfold vajra-yogas" refers to those which destroy the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state; they are the vajra-yogas purified as form, mantra, dharma, and reality, and have the nature of the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya), enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya), dharma body (dharmakāya), and great bliss body (mahāsukhakāya), consisting of the unobscured body, speech, mind, and gnosis.

"By the four types of awakening" means by the awakenings through the *māyājāla* consisting of one moment, five aspects, and twenty aspects. "By the six families of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases" means by the purification of Vairocana, Amitābha, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amoghasiddhi, Akṣobhya, and Vajrasattva, corresponding to the six aggregates of form, perception, feeling, mental formations, consciousness, and gnosis. [This occurs] through the purification of Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, Tārā, Vajradhātvīśvarī, and Prajñāpāramitā.

By means of the six elements—earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness; by the term "āyatana," the sense organs, their objects, the organs of action, and their activities are included; and therein, by means of the purification of Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, Lokeśvara, Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Samantabhadra, Viśuddhi, and [the deities of] the body, tongue, eye, nose, ear, and mind—the six sense organs.

Through the purification of the Vajra of Odor, the Vajra of Form, the Vajra of Taste, the Vajra of Touch, the Vajra of the Dharmadhātu, and the Vajra of Sound, there are six [faculties] consisting of odor, form, taste, touch, the dharmadhātu, and sound. Through the purification of Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, Vighnāntaka, Uṣṇīṣa, and Śumbha, there are six [organs] consisting of the anus, feet, hands, speech, genitals, and the divine organ of action.

Through the purification of the goddesses Stambhī, Mānī, Jambhī, Ativīryā, Atinīlā, and Raudrākṣī—the wrathful goddesses—by means of the six functions of the male organ: speaking, giving, moving, discharging feces, emitting semen, and passing urine; and through the five chapters consisting of the chapters on the World System, the Internal, the Empowerment, the Means of Achievement, and the Gnosis; this Tantra is pure and endowed with these qualities, such as the six points [of interpretation]. It is purified by the two truths, the conventional and the ultimate; it teaches all mundane and supramundane gnosis; it is free from attachment to the two sides [of existence and non-existence]; and it is the Primordial Buddha, without beginning or end.

"Because of the syllable *kā*, the cause is pacified; because of the syllable *la*, there is indeed dissolution (*laya*) here; because of the syllable *ca*, the flickering mind [is stilled]; and because of the syllable *kra*, there is release from the bondage of succession. Having established this, it is designated as the *Kālacakra*.
Water, and so forth: O King, the sevenfold consecration consists of water, the crown, the ribbon, the vajra-bell, the great vow, together with the name and the authorization. (10)
The purification of body, speech, and mind constitutes two initiations each;
the permission initiation is the purification of gnosis, while the others arise from the purification of the elements and so forth. (11)
The water is the purification of the elements; the crown is the purification of the aggregates;
the ribbon is the purification of the perfections; and the vajra-bell is the great syllable.
The speech of the Buddha is uninterrupted; it is the purification of the sun and moon into one.
The complete purification of the objects and the senses is the infallible Vajra-vow. (13)
The purification of the name is the purification through loving-kindness and so forth; the permission (*anujñā*) is the purification of the Buddha.

Immediately after bestowing the vows of a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*) and so on, outside the eastern gate of the maṇḍala, following the giving of the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), and after the throwing of flowers upon the victory-vase (*jayaghaṭa*) marked with the symbols of the families of the five Tathāgatas, there are two sets of two consecrations—water and so forth—at the northern, southern, and eastern gates of the maṇḍala, according to the method stated in the *Śrīvimalaprabhā-ṭīkā*. At the western gate is the permission.

The consecration (*abhiṣeka*). "Other" refers to another purification of the elements, aggregates, and so forth, which results from the purification of the body and so on. "Vajra-bell" refers to the consecration of the vajra and bell. In that context, the vajra is purified by the great immutable gnosis (*akṣara-jñāna*); the bell is purified by the uninterrupted speech of the Buddha; the meaning is that it is purified by the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*) resonance. "The purification of the unity of sun and moon" means that the gesture of embracing these very two—the vajra and the bell—is for the purpose of indicating the non-duality of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). "These," and so forth...
These seven empowerments should be bestowed after having drawn the mandala.

The seven consecrations are to be bestowed upon the dust mandala alone; they are not [bestowed] upon a mandala such as one painted on cloth, because the Blessed One did not mention them in the tantras.
The vase, the secret consecration, and that which is designated as the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna);
furthermore, the great wisdom and the knowledge designated as belonging to it. || 15 ||
The perishable, the imperishable, from that the vibration, and beyond that the non-vibration;
through the purification of body, speech, and mind, there are the three consecrations in sequence. (16)
The fourth is the complete purification of gnosis, which purifies body, speech, and mind;
he is the child, the youth, and likewise the elder, while the fourth is Prajāpati. (17)
From the contact with the limbs of the Wisdom Consort’s breasts, there is the bliss of the emission of bodhicitta;
he is "consecrated by the breasts" (payodharābhiṣikta), because he has attained that bliss which is [the state of] the Child (bāla). 18.
The bliss born from the striking of the secret place after a long time is the emission of the thought of awakening;
he is maturely consecrated in the secret, because the bliss was obtained from the secret. (19)
From the striking of the secret place, the bliss born after a long time throbs at the tip of the vajra;
for that elder, having been consecrated by the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna), has attained vibration. (20)
That bliss which arises from the lack of movement through passion for Mahāmudrā is the consecration of Great Wisdom, because it has attained the state of non-fluctuation. || 21 ||
He is to be known as Prajāpati, the progenitor of all protectors;
he is Vajrasattva, Mahāsattva, the non-dual and immutable Bodhisattva. (22)
This is the Samayasattva, the fourfold Vajrayoga;
here it is known as Kālacakra, the bestower of liberation upon yogins. (23)

With the words "Kumbha," and so forth [15a], he indicates the ritual of offering the *kumbha* and other items by means of the words "the breast-limb of wisdom," and so forth [18a]. Furthermore, with the words "Again indeed," and so forth [15b], he indicates the supramundane fourth great wisdom-knowledge consecration (*mahājñānābhiṣeka*) by means of the words "the Great Seal" (*mahāmudrā*), and so forth [21a]. Now, immediately after the statement of the result, he speaks of the path for its accomplishment with the words "of this," and so forth [24a]:
"One should perform the accomplishment of this very [path] through inconceivable manifestations."
By means of those signs such as smoke and others, which are reflections of wisdom equal to the sky. || 24 ||
By means of the objects of cognition that have transcended existence and non-existence, and by one's own mind which is entirely devoid of even the slightest accumulation of atoms; || 25 ||
Through smoke, mirage, fireflies, lamp, flame, moon, and sun,
[one perceives] darkness, the digit, the great bindu, the luminous reflection of the universe.

"Of this" refers to Vajrasattva, whose nature is supreme great bliss (*anuttara-mahāsukha*) in which the four bodies have become one, free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). "By means of the images of wisdom" (*prajñābimba*) means by means of the forms that are reflections of wisdom, which is non-conceptual and of the nature of supreme wisdom; they are inseparable, like the moon and its moonlight. "Smoke," and so forth, up to "lamp"—the yogi perceives these four signs within the cave (*guhā*) as non-conceptualized, through inconceivable gnosis (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, one perceives the six signs in open space, beginning with the flame and ending with the drop. Thereafter, one perceives the image in all its aspects, non-conceptual, like a dream-appearance. Now, with the verse beginning "With eyes closed" (pihitā), he explains the sequence of meditating on the universal image:
"With eyes both closed and open, that which is not mentally constructed in the void is seen as an image like a dream; one should always meditate upon that image. (27)
When there is no mental image (*bimba*), that meditation is not meditation for yogins;
for the mind has neither existence nor non-existence when it perceives the image without conceptual construction. (28)

With the verse beginning with "non-existence" (abhāva), he provides the proof for the negation of the cultivation characterized by the repeated superimposition of mental constructs. In that context, "not imagined" refers to that which is non-conceptualized in the beginning, middle, and end. Therein, "non-existence" is used because the ultimate cultivation has a nature unmarked by the stains of all conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). For this very reason, he says: "Existence and non-existence do not belong to the mind, because there is the vision of the non-imagined in the image."

How, then, does the universal image appear to the yogin? Therefore, he provides an illustration with the words beginning with “like a *pratisenā*”: “Just as a young girl might see in a mirror a *pratisenā* that is not a real thing, so too the yogin sees past and future phenomena even in the sky. (29)

The descent of the *pratisenā* (magical mirror-image) is said to occur in eight [media]: in a mirror, a sword, a thumb, a lamp, the moon, the sun, water, and the eye. Among these, the mirror is mentioned here. That *pratisenā* is what is contemplated by the practitioner. This is the intended meaning: just as in a mirror there appears to a young girl the unconstructed reflection (*avikalpita-pratibhāsa*) of objects such as thieves, whether past, future, or present, in exactly the same way, for the yogin as well, because all the dust of conceptual construction has departed from the sky [of the mind], there appears the reflection of the entire universe (*viśvabimba*) as stainless and non-conceptual.

This very [nature] is elsewhere called the "emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects. To negate the adherence to this very image as being ultimate reality, he states the following example beginning with "Of this...
"Of this, existence would not be existence, because of seeing the meaning of the emptiness of things;
yet, due to the non-existence of the thing, its object exists like an illusion, a dream, or a magical display. (30)

"The nature of this *pratisenā* (magical vision) is neither existence nor non-existence," because, like an illusion, it is the appearance of an entity that is unarisen by its own nature (*svabhāva*). To dispel the doubt—namely, "How then can the Blessed One’s activity for the sake of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) proceed from a cognition that is free from all conceptual construction?"—he states an illustration beginning with the words "asati" (when there is no [entity]):
"When there is no substratum (*dharmin*), this arising of a property (*dharma*) is indeed observed, Like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), fulfilling the needs of infinite sentient beings. (31)

Just as a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) performs the welfare of sentient beings while being devoid of conceptual construction, so too it is not contradictory for the Blessed One—who is free from all discursive thought and has attained infinite qualities such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses—to perform the welfare of all sentient beings. Now, he states the non-deceptiveness of gnosis: "The unseen," and so forth.
[32] A young girl sees thieves and the like in a mirror-image divination (pratisenā), even though they are unseen;
then practitioners go and see them with their own limited eyes. [32]

In this regard, just as a young girl sees thieves and the like in a mirror without conceptual construction (*avikalpita*), so too do limited beings, having gone to the places described by the girl, actually encounter those thieves and so forth. Likewise, for the practitioner of reality (*tattvayogin*), the vision of the triple world (*traidhātuka*) without conceptual construction becomes beneficial for the sake of sentient beings. Furthermore, in order to dispel the insistence on whether that which appears as the form of an object is existent or non-existent, he says "If...
and so forth: "If she sees what has the nature of being real, why does she not see her own face? [33]
If one perceives that which has the form of a non-existent thing, why does one not perceive a rabbit's horn? (33)

If, first of all, a real entity (*vastu*) appears, then why does the girl’s face, which is actually present and adjacent to the mirror, not appear? Nor does a non-existent entity appear, because a rabbit's horn—characterized by absolute non-existence—is not perceived. This is what is meant: an entity such as an illusion (*māyā*), free from the dogmatic attachment to conceptual constructions of existence, non-existence, and so forth, appears and performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*). Now, in order to dispel the dogmatic attachment to seeing through the sense faculties such as the eye, he says: "He does not see," and so forth.
One does not see with another's eyes, nor does one see with one's own eyes;
that which is being seen is unborn, just like the birth of a barren woman's son.

"By the other two eyes" means by those located on the forehead and so forth; he does not see with his own two eyes because they are covered by a blindfold. This is the intended meaning: even the perception of an object free from conceptual construction and attachment is not contradictory, just like the seeing in a dream. For this very reason, he states the analogy with the words "being seen," and so forth.
Withdrawal, as well as meditative concentration, breath control, retention, recollection, and meditative absorption—this is considered the six-limbed yoga. (GST 18.141)

By the statement beginning with "one should perform the sādhana of this very [deity]" and ending with "just as the birth [of the deity] occurs for a maiden," two limbs—known as withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)—are taught through the vision of the image in all its aspects without conceptualization, by way of the underlying meaning. Now, the two limbs known as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and retention (*dhāraṇā*) are described:
"Once the image has been seen, one should then perform breath control continuously, by obstructing body, speech, and mind within the three channels above and below. (35)
In those that carry the flow of the moon, sun, Rāhu, feces, urine, and semen;
and in those born from the elements of water, fire, space, earth, wind, and consciousness. || 36 ||

The channels of body, speech, and mind—namely moon, sun, and darkness—are, respectively, the carriers of feces, urine, and semen, corresponding to the ascending (prāṇa) and descending (apāna) breaths. 37.

When the image is seen—that is, when the image in all its aspects, which is non-conceptual, has been seen—[the term] *prāṇāyāma* refers to the entry into the middle [channel], Rāhu, due to the halting of the movement of the vital winds (*prāṇavāyu*) on the paths of the moon and the sun. When the vital wind is gradually restrained within the wheels (*cakra*) starting from the navel and so forth, precisely in the *avadhūtī*, that is called *dhāraṇā*. Regarding "in the channels" (*nāḍīṣu*), this refers to the *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī*, which carry feces, urine, and semen; "by way of restraint" (*avarodhanāt*) means by way of making them free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇīkaraṇāt*) of the *lalanā* and other channels.

Thus, by means of the two verses beginning with "The Moon" (candra) [verses 36 and 37], the specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is to be understood according to their respective order, because they are the birthplaces of the elements such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth. *Tamini* is the middle channel of Rāhu. Now, he establishes the six families (*ṣaṭkula*) through the three verses beginning with "The Moon is Body" [verse 38], by means of the division of body, speech, and mind within those very [channels] as wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*).
The moon is the body of skillful means, while the sun is the speech of wisdom;
the feces-channel is the body of wisdom, and the urine-carrying channel is the speech of the pervasive Lord.
Both the upper and lower [channels] are the flows of darkness and semen for the mind;
Taminī is the mind of method, while the Śukravāhinī belongs to wisdom. (39)
Indeed, these six families above and below exist in all embodied beings through the union of body, speech, and mind, established by way of the factors of wisdom and means. (40)

In this context, "of the means" refers to the semen element; "of the wisdom" refers to the blood element. Death occurs when the winds excessively increase in the upper and lower channels of body and speech, resulting in the arising, abiding, and death within the channels that carry *tamiṇī* and semen. (41)
At the time of birth, death, and sexual intercourse, the *śukravāhinī* flows; however, during the equinox (*viṣuva*) at the transit of the sun, the *tamini* flows upward.
And at the junction of the rising of the ascendant, O King, the central equinoctial flow consists of six hundred and fifty with a quarter in both its entry and exit. (43)
With six hundred and seventy-five [days] more, day and night;
and also that which is twenty-one thousand plus six hundred. || 44 ||
By this [process], the two flowing channels, the left and the right, [function] for three fortnights and three years; and the middle channel [functions] for one hundred years.
*Vāmā* is on the upper left; *candra* and *arka* are *lalanā* and *iḍā*, while *pingalā* is the other.

"Ariṣṭam" is the introductory term for the *ariṣṭa* (signs of death) that will be explained later. "Of the sun" refers to the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*). "At the junction of the rising of the ascendant" means between the *lalanā* and *rasanā*. "Equinox" (*viṣuva*) refers to the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇavāha*) consisting of fifty-six and a quarter breaths within the *avadhūtī*. By these twelve [breaths], there are six hundred and seventy-five breaths in one day and night. "By this" refers to the six hundred and seventy-five breaths.

Regarding the passage beginning with *satripakṣa* [45b]: from the heap of breaths consisting of seven hundred minus one-quarter (*pāda*), multiplied by the heap of days in a hundred years, one obtains a quotient by dividing by twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths per day. From that heap, the portions obtained by dividing by three hundred and sixty—excluding the remainder of the division as lost days—constitute the three years and three-and-a-half months (*satripakṣa*) in the *madhyamā*. The hundred years devoid of these belong to the *lalanā* and *rasanā*. Regarding the passage beginning with *vāmā savyordhva* [46]: "above" means above the navel; the *vāmā* is named *candra* and *iḍā*, while the *savyā* is *arka*.

And another is named Piṅgalā, and the one above is named Rasanā. Now, with two and a half verses, he explains the purification of the Tathāgata families for the channels (nāḍī) such as Lalanā, which are purified of the elements beginning with water:
"Those whose natures are water and fire are considered to be Padmadhṛk and Ratnadhṛk. (46)
Below are the two channels carrying feces and urine, which have the natures of earth and air respectively;
the central channel and the left one alone are considered to be the wielder of the discus and the wielder of the sword.
The upper [channel] and the middle one below the left are Rāhu and Śukra-pravāhikā;
they have the nature of emptiness and gnosis, and are considered to be Vajradhṛk and Vajradhṛṅ. (48)

In this context, Padmadhrk and the others are to be understood as Amitābha and the rest. The "central channel" (*madhyanāḍī*) is that which carries feces in its lower portion. The "left" (*vāmā*) is the channel situated on the left at the base of the *vajra*, which carries urine. The "right" (*savyā*) is the one situated on the right at that very same place, which carries semen. By the term "second Vajradhrk," the sixth, Vajrasattva, is meant. Because the channels of the Moon, Sun, and Rāhu situated above the navel are engaged in the activity of carrying feces and so forth, they become the "feces-channel" and so on; this is shown by the verse beginning with "feces" (*viṭ*). The feces-channel flows by way of the Moon-path, while the urine-carrying channel flows by way of the Sun.
At the equinoxes of birth and death, Rāhu and Venus carry [the breath].
With the verse beginning "That which is above the navel," he states another designation for the *avadhūtī* and the *śukravāhinī*:
"That which is the *avadhūtī* above the navel is the *suṣumnā*, the carrier of darkness (*tamas*).
And that which is below, the carrier of semen, is the *khagamukhā* and the *śaṅkhinī*. (50)

With these two verses beginning with "In the navel-lotus" (nābhyabja), he explains that the Avadhūtī, by virtue of having the nature of the five elements, possesses the nature of withdrawal, creation, entry, and exit. "In the navel-lotus, the heart, the throat, and the lotuses of the forehead and the crown, she flows through withdrawal as earth, water, fire, wind, and space. (51)
Emerging and aiming [toward the goal], she enters the earth by means of emanation;
having been drawn up from one pericarp into the middle of another pericarp, there is the coming and going.

In the same way, with the two verses beginning with "not non-existence" (nābhāva), he describes the sequence of the flow within the *śaṅkhinī* by means of the dharmas of body, speech, and mind: "At the navel and at the secret place, in the lotus of the jewel, the channels of body, speech, and mind flow."
Emerging and piercing through, she takes the form of both dissolution and creation.
The Śaṅkhinī carries the downward-voiding wind (apānavāyu) of all sentient beings;
and it is this very channel that, in women during their fertile period, carries semen and blood for the sake of pleasure.

"This" refers to the channel that carries semen (*śukra*). By means of the verse beginning with "wisdom and method" (verse 55), the state of wisdom and method is described through the embrace of the other family by the six family channels, such as *lalanā* and the rest:
"By way of being limbs of wisdom and method, they are above on the right and left;
below, they carry feces and urine, while [the others] carry the flow of *rajas* and semen. (55)
Caṇḍālī is known as the carrier of the female menses, while Khagamukhā is the carrier of semen;
in women, she is remembered as Ḍombī during the fertile period (ṛtu), whereas in men, she is Avadhūtī.

"Because of the flow of *rajas* (menstrual blood), the *Candālī*... and so forth. First, for women, due to the pleasure arising from the flow of *rajas*, the designations "Candālī" and "Ḍombī" apply to the *Śaṅkhinī* and *Avadhūtī* channels. For men as well, these names are applied figuratively because the body arises precisely through contact with *rajas*. By the verse beginning with "Consciousness and so forth" [57], he indicates the specific divisions of the flow of the aggregates such as consciousness and the elements such as earth within the left and right nostrils:
"Consciousness and the others, as five mandalas, should always be in the left channel."
Earth and the other elements flow in the right channel; then, the sixth element flows again in the middle.
In the center, within the *avadhūtī*, is the sixth, the mandala of gnosis (*jñāna*). There are sixty mandalas on the petals of the navel-lotus, and so forth.
On the petals of the navel-lotus there are sixty mandalas in their respective order, situated on the left and right, corresponding to Aries and the others, and Taurus and the others. (58)

In one day and night, through the transition of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) at each successive ascendant (*lagna*) starting from Aries and Taurus, by means of five and five *maṇḍalas* of the sixty *daṇḍas*—distinguished as uneven and even—the twelve equinoctial transitions (*viṣuva-saṃkrānti*) occur at the navel and in the two nostrils; this is the intended meaning. With the words beginning "at the root" (*mūla*), he describes the locations of the vital breath according to the nature of earth and the other elements:
"At the root, then on the left, then on the right, above, and in the middle, the wind (*anila*) proceeds in sequence.
One *daṇḍa* corresponds to each single *maṇḍala*, beginning with earth, in the two nostrils. (59)
A single nāḍī successively carries three hundred and sixty breaths;
five nāḍīs carry one thousand eight hundred breaths.
Sixty *daṇḍas* constitute a day and night; these are the mandalas according to the body.
Then, in the middle of the petals, they are placed in sequence: in the east, the right, the left, and the west. (61)
Space and the others are always on the left; earth and the others are on the right from the other [side].
Consciousness and the others are emanation on the left; earth and the others are withdrawal on the right.

In that context, "at the root" (*mūle*) means at the lower part of both nostrils. "On the left" (*vāme*) means at the region of the nasal septum between the two. In this way, the sequence beginning with the left should be understood for the outer, upper, and middle parts. "From the body" (*dehataḥ*) means from the navel. By the phrase "in the middle of the petal" (*dalamadhye*) and so forth, he shows the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇavāha*) which first arose in the left nostril by way of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other aggregates. "In front" (*pūrve*) means above; "behind" (*apare*) means at the lower part.

Regarding the phrase "beginning with space" (ākāśādyam) [62], because the aggregates beginning with consciousness arise from the elements beginning with space, their non-difference is shown by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). For this very reason, it was previously stated: "beginning with earth, in the two nostrils" [59]. Regarding the statement "beginning with earth, from the lower part of the right" [62a], this refers to the lower portion of the right nostril. Here, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which first arose as beginning with earth, flows; in this context, this very direction is the east.

Because of the statement, "The sunrise is in the east; the movement is equal to the mountain" (LKCT 1.61a), one might ask: since the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) arises in the space of the left nostril, how is it that space is not considered the east? It is not so, because among the four directions, the middle point cannot be designated as "east" and so forth. For this very reason, he indicates the east there as being above the nostril. "Bhava" refers to emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).

Now, with the four verses beginning with "The other" (pare) [verse 63], he explains the mutual nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*) for earth and wind, fire and water, and space and the element of consciousness, by means of the instruction on the mudrās such as the offering of the thumb and ring finger. "The other" refers to the preceding: earth and wind are wisdom and method respectively. And because the consecration occurs in the mouth by means of the thumb and ring finger. (63)
Fire is on the right and water on the left; wisdom and means are mutually [joined].
Since the sword shall arise from the middle and index fingers, [it is so called]. (64)
The void syllable is above and below; wisdom and means are mutually [united].
The two half-moon shapes are the fang-seal (*daṃṣṭrāmudrā*); the small finger is the knife. (65)
The joining of the ten circles of the fingers with one another,
through the union of the palms at the crown of the head, is the *ekaśūka* [mudrā] together with the *kartikā*.
The equinox occurs in the central channel, effecting both creation and dissolution;
when the three vajras of the aggregates and elements reach the central channel, they become one.

In this context, because the thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger, and little finger are purified as earth, water, fire, wind, and space respectively, the purity of wisdom and method is to be understood through the binding of the mudrā. "The syllable" refers to the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*). "The union of the ten maṇḍalas" refers to the unity of the aggregates and elements. "Single-pronged" refers to the single-pronged vajra. "With a knife" indicates the nature of the aggregates and elements—which have been pierced by Vajrasattva together with Prajñā—becoming a single, unified mass.

Now, for the purpose of concluding by means of describing the characteristics of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and retention (*dhāraṇā*), breath control is indicated by the half-verse beginning with "In the moon" (68a). Retention is explained by the half-verse beginning with "By Rāhu" (68b). The fault in the opposite case is stated by the half-verse beginning with "The pearls" (69a). Through the obstruction of the lunar and solar channels, the channels of feces and urine are obstructed; through the downward obstruction of the Rāhu channel, the flow of semen is obstructed. (68)
These [energies], which effect creation and dissolution, become liberated in liberation;
such is the movement of the channels through the three paths of prāṇa and apāna. (69)

Now, he explains both types of *ariṣṭa* previously mentioned with the verse beginning with "vāmā" and so forth: "If the wind flows for one night or five nights in either the left or the right [nostril], then death will occur in three years. (70)
Fifty-five days is the ascent of the principles (tattva) in a sequence of one per day;
this is the thirty-three-day ascent by the sun when the fatal sign (ariṣṭa) occurs on the right.
The lifespan of embodied beings has passed away in three, two, or one months; six, three, two, or one days; and fifteen, ten, five, three, two, or one lunar days (tithis). || 72 ||

With the two verses beginning with "five" (pañca), he describes the signs of death from the sun (*sūryāriṣṭa*). Herein is the meaning: when, due to an imbalance of the elements in sentient beings, the wind flows uninterruptedly for five days and nights through the right nostril—the basis of the equal junction—then death has arisen, indicating a lifespan of three years.

Then, due to the movement through the ten maṇḍalas within the twelve petals consisting of the twelve zodiac signs located at the navel, the wind flows by means of a corresponding conveyance, having subtracted three hundred and thirty days from the three years; subsequently, having taken two years and twenty-five days, the wind moves in the second petal, flowing uninterruptedly for ten days and nights in the right nostril.

Then, having subtracted three hundred and thirty-five days according to the *yathāyogavāha* [method], and having taken one year plus a month and ten days, it moves into the third petal. There, in that petal, it carries misfortune (*ariṣṭa*) for fifteen days and nights. Then, having subtracted one hundred and fifty-five days according to the *yathāyogavāha*, and having taken seven months plus twenty days, it moves into the fourth petal. It carries misfortune for twenty days.

Then, having subtracted two months and two days according to the *yathāyogavāha* [method], one takes four months and twenty-eight days; [the breath] circulates in the fifth petal. It carries the *ariṣṭa* for twenty-five days. Then, [it remains] for one month and two days.

Having subtracted two days according to the *yathāyogavāha* [calculation], and having taken two months and three days, it moves through the sixth petal; it carries the *ariṣṭa* for twenty-six days. Then, having subtracted two days according to the *yathāyogavāha*, and having taken two months and three days, it moves through the seventh petal; here it carries the *ariṣṭa* for twenty-seven days. Thereafter, in the eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh petals, it carries the *ariṣṭa* continuously for fifteen, ten, five, and three days respectively.

When the five petals beginning with the seventh are abandoned, it does not flow according to its usual course. Thenceforth, it flows for two days in the left nostril at the twelve-petalled [lotus], and for one day in the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Furthermore, regarding the group of days of three years—characterized by the omen of misfortune (*ariṣṭa*)—amounting to one thousand eighty days, plus three hundred and thirty-five days and so forth, the flow of the initial five days of misfortune occurs right at the beginning in the first six petals, following the sequence of abandonment of each petal.

Afterwards, outside of that day, the movement according to the appropriate application should be understood from the three hundred and thirty days and so forth mentioned previously. And likewise, there is a verse explaining the abandonment of the daily life-force days along with the days of *ariṣṭa* (fatal signs) in the case of Śrī-Ādibuddha: "First, one abandons a group of days equal to five hundred and three; thereafter, indeed, [one abandons] sixty-four; and in the third [period], fifty-three."
"Eye, snake, mountain, arrow; another is eight-fingered, and Rohaṇa in the seventh;

from that, all the lunar days and so forth, as well as the total number of days, up to the pericarp. (LKCT 2.64) Furthermore, the lifespan, years, months, and so forth mentioned by the verse beginning with "three, two, one, equal," etc., is a coarse measurement. From the aforementioned explanation, its subtle division should again be understood. This concludes the explanation of the solar *ariṣṭa*. Now, with the half-verse beginning with "the root," etc., he speaks of the lunar *ariṣṭa*.
From the base, the ascent of the moon occurs on the left by increments of one:
by days and months, by days and months, and by three months and three days. (73)

In the days and months of misfortune (*ariṣṭa*), due to their increase and then their decrease, when the wind flows uninterruptedly day and night through that left nostril (*vāmanāsāpuṭa*) while resting in an odd zodiac sign (*viṣamalagna*), then the lunar misfortune (*candrāriṣṭa*) has arisen, indicating a lifespan of three years. Thereafter, it flows according to the circumstances, moving through ten circles (*maṇḍala*) during the first and second months, which are diminished by the number of days of misfortune. Then, upon entering the third month, it flows as a misfortune for two days. After that, it flows according to the circumstances during the third and fourth months, which are diminished by two days.

Then, upon entering the fifth month, it carries misfortune (ariṣṭa) for three days. Thereafter, it proceeds through the fifth and sixth months minus those three days, according to the appropriate application. It abandons the first petal among the twelve petals consisting of the twelve zodiac signs located at the navel. Having abandoned six months out of three years and taken up the remaining thirty months, it moves into the second petal. Upon the entry into the seventh, eighth, and ninth months, it carries misfortune for four, five, and six days respectively.

Then, having subtracted three months less the days of misfortune (*ariṣṭa*) from the monthly [count] according to the *yathāyogavāha* method, and taking twenty-seven months, it moves in the third petal. By this very sequence, having subtracted three months with an increase of three days of misfortune, [it moves] in the seventh [petal].

It abandons [the body] after twenty-one days of misfortune (*ariṣṭa*). In that regard, at the beginning of the entry into the three months to be abandoned, having applied the respective flow within each set of three months—diminished by twenty-four, twenty-seven, thirty, and thirty-three days of misfortune—it abandons the eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh petals. Therein, for the three days not yet traversed belonging to the six months associated with the first abandoned petal, the misfortune flows for two days in the right nostril on the twelfth petal.

For one day, [the breath] remains in the pericarp (*karṇikā*); there occurs the cessation of all winds, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) departs to another world. This concludes the *Candrāriṣṭavyākhyā*.
With the two and a half verses beginning with "madhyamā" [74b], he describes the intermediate time of death:
"The intermediate ascent of death occurs when one hundred years are fully completed. (74)
The ascent upon those [circles] occurs by means of equal and unequal days, through the mandalas born of one's birth,
on the right and the left, due to the destruction of both fortnights.
Otherwise, death would not occur, because of the persistence of both sides [of the breath] through the movement of the left and right channels and the flow of the five maṇḍalas. (76)

Therein, for ninety-six years plus ten and a half months related to the moon and sun, the wind flows uninterruptedly for one day in the left nostril, presiding over time. Then, through the movement of the ten mandalas, it flows for one day according to its appropriate course. Thereafter, it flows uninterruptedly for two days in the right nostril, and likewise again for two days according to its appropriate course.

Thus, based on the distinction between the uneven and even [flows] in the left and right nostril passages, it flows for three, four, five, and six days. It abandons the space and earth mandalas of the left and right [nostrils]. By means of the movement through the left and right exactly in the stated order, it flows for seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, and twelve days. Then it abandons the wind and water mandalas. Likewise, for thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, and eighteen days, it abandons the fire and light mandalas.

In this manner, it abandons the water and wind mandalas during nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, and twenty-four days. Likewise, it flows for twenty-five, twenty-six, twenty-seven, twenty-eight, twenty-nine, and thirty days, abandoning the earth and space mandalas. Similarly, it flows for thirty-one, thirty-two, and thirty-three days, and abandons the gnosis mandala as well.

Then it flows uninterruptedly through the right nostril for thirty-three days; for one day in the pericarp (*karṇikā*). After that, there shall be an interruption of all the elements (*dhātu*s). By the end of those thirty-three days, including the auspicious and inauspicious days and lunar mansions (*rāśi*), there are one thousand two hundred and twenty-two days. Including the thirty-three days of uninterrupted flow in the right nostril along with the day in the pericarp, there would be one thousand one hundred and fifty-six days.
An Explanation of Intermediate Time Death.

Having known the signs of death (*ariṣṭalakṣaṇa*), and so forth—through these three verses [77], he teaches the instruction on deceiving death (*ariṣṭavañcana*). Furthermore, that instruction is to be understood only from the mouth of the Guru; therefore, no detailed exposition of it has been made here.
Having recognized the signs of impending death, one should cause the vital breath to enter the *bindu*;
having taken recourse to the station of the *avadhūtī*, one should meditate upon the supreme syllable.
One should always effect the vajra-arising by breaking the movement of the moon and sun;
otherwise, the vital wind does not enter the avadhūtī channel. (78)
The apāna [wind] moves downward into the śaṅkhinī; from its non-entry there occurs death. This is the deception of the omens of death (ariṣṭa) for yogins, which occurs through the blisses. || 79 ||
From the statement, "It shall become bliss for yogins," the question arises: "What is this bliss? In response, he explains the classification of the blisses:
"The non-arrival of the semen is bliss (*ānanda*) from the *uṣṇīṣa* to the lotus of the *ūrṇā*;
at the throat and heart it is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), and thereafter viramānanda shall arise. (80)
Since the various delights have gone from the navel to the secret lotus, there is the infallible innate bliss (sahajānanda) within the secret vajra-jewel. 81.

By these two verses beginning with "śukra," the limb of *anusmṛti* (recollection) is indicated through the description of the characteristics of bliss (*ānanda*). With the half-verse beginning "apratiṣṭhitanirvāṇam," he indicates the limb of *samādhi* (meditative concentration):
"Apratiṣṭhitanirvāṇa is great passion, the immutable Lord.
That bliss which has fallen away from passion is a nirvāṇa that is established. (82)

"Non-abiding nirvāṇa" refers to that which is non-abiding at the forehead; having not emerged from the vajra, it has become a single fusion with the three vajras—the great bliss of innate joy (*sahajānanda*). Beyond this, he describes its specific qualities through many verses concerning recollection (*anusmṛti*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*): "The rising of the moon of semen at the crown, full in the secret lotus;
that sixteenth digit which is in the jewel-lotus, it goes to the tip of the vajra. (83)
Thereafter, at the arrival of the first day of the dark fortnight, the time of descent occurs;
however, due to detachment, on the new moon day, the sun has reached the station of the *ūrṇā*.
And its sixteenth digit has gone to the uṣṇīṣa-lotus;
it is known as the "lost moon," a state of detachment from the bliss of passion. (85)

This is the meaning: here, just as in the external world, due to the increase of the digits (*kalā*) of the lunar days (*tithi*) beginning with the first (*pratipad*), there occurs for the risen moon the triad of the fifth, tenth, and fifteenth [days] as full; and the sixteenth digit, which exists at the end of the bright fortnight and the middle of the beginning of the dark fortnight, is not a digit, according to the statement: "because it is not a digit" (cf. HT II.iv.27).

Likewise, within the internal [body], the moon of the bodhicitta that has arisen at the *uṣṇīṣa* becomes the triad of the fifth, tenth, and fifteenth—the full [moon]—respectively at the forehead, the heart, and the secret lotus, according to the divisions of bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth. The sixteenth digit (*kalā*), which exists between the end of passion and the beginning of dispassion, resides at the crown of the *vajra*; it is characterized by non-abiding nirvāṇa and is designated by the term "innate bliss" (*sahajānanda*). Thus it is also said in the *Hevajra*: "The bodhicitta is the moon, consisting of fifteen digits."

"The form of Āli is great bliss, and the Yoginīs are its portions" (HT II.iv.29). Here, "the sun" refers to the element of *rajas* (ovum); "the place of the *ūrṇā*" refers to the lotus of the forehead. "Of that" refers to the sun and *rajas*. Just as there occurs a specific state among sentient beings during sexual union, so too at the time of death;
this he demonstrates with the words beginning, "downward, the nectar of the moon," for all embodied beings at the moment of death, the nectar of the moon goes downward.
Above, in the characteristic of existence, are the sun, dust, Rāhu, and consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "characterized by existence" (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*), it refers to the characteristic of arising due to the power of karmic latencies (*karmavāsanā*). With the two verses beginning with "Therefore," he demonstrates the opposite of that.
Therefore, O King, the movement of the lunar nectar (*candrāmṛta*) must be made upward;
the downward movement of the solar dust (*arkarajas*), of Rāhu, and of consciousness (*vijñāna*) [must be made] into the immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*). (87)
In the ūrṇā-lotus of all Buddhas, there is the full moon of nectar; in the secret place, it is the new moon of solar dust; and in the uṣṇīṣa and the jewel, it is the digit (kalā) of both.

"Of those two" refers to the moon and sun of *bodhicitta* and *rajas*. The venerable feet of Lokeśvara have expressed this very same meaning by way of a salutation: "Having bowed my head to the Lord, who is honored by the three worlds—I place one foot upon the *vajramaṇi*, the sun of *rajas*, and the second upon the moon of the *uṣṇīṣa*-semen; thus it is eternally indestructible, indivisible, and desired. (VP, ed., Vol. I, p. 3, ll. 5–6)
Thus, this vajra-word of the Teacher is the opposite for all embodied beings;
and because of non-abiding nirvāṇa, the elements are likewise the opposite. (89)

"From non-abiding nirvāṇa" means from non-conceptual, untainted great bliss (*nirvikalpānāśravamahāsukha*). "The opposite," and so forth, means that the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases attain a state of being non-conceptual and free from obscuration in all their aspects; this is the meaning. However, according to other [interpretations], because of the statement beginning with "form and so forth," he now describes the radiation from below the navel of the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*—which are connected to the means (*upāya*)—through the purification of mind, speech, and body, from the body of great bliss purified as the *jñānavajra*.
He states this in the verse beginning with "The mind in the jewel" (*maṇau cittaṃ*), which consists of one and a quarter stanzas.
The mind is in the jewel, speech in the secret place, and the body in the navel; from great bliss, those bodies of Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation radiate forth from the pure state. (90)
O King of Kings, the means (upāya) is below and wisdom (prajñā) is above;
her body-vajra (kāyavajra) is located in the forehead, throat, heart, and navel lotuses. 91.
Indeed, the vajras of speech, mind, and gnosis emanate from the [body] of emanation and so forth; this emanation of the aggregates and elements arises from unobscured bliss. (92)

In that context, by the phrase "of the means" (*upāya*), which refers to the bodhicitta associated with the father, and likewise "of the wisdom" (*prajñā*) and so forth, he describes the emanation from the body-vajra—the pure nirmāṇakāya—above the navel, of the speech-vajra and other bodies such as the saṃbhogakāya, which are purified. By "of the wisdom," he refers to the *rajas* element associated with the mother.

Because of the predominance of the qualities of the gnosis of great bliss—which consists of means characterized by non-referential compassion—and the gnosis of emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects, it is taught that there is a distinct radiation of the innate [body] and so forth, as well as the emanation [body] and so forth, respectively. However, in ultimate reality, there would be no separate differentiation of the bodies and so on.

"Through union with the action-seal (karmamudrā), through reliance on the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā), and through the singular yoga of the great seal (mahāmudrā), that imperishable [bliss] increases. (93)

With the verse beginning "Karmamudrā" [93a], he explains the means for increasing the non-conceptual great bliss wisdom (*nirvikalpa-mahāsukha-jñāna*) that has arisen from the cultivation of Mahāmudrā. Alternatively, the three mudrās and the three fruits have been taught. And so it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "The fruit of accomplishment belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) is produced by the cause of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*); the fruit of accomplishment belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) is produced by the cause of the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*)."

The fruit, which is the accomplishment of non-conceptual omniscience, is produced by the cause that is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects. For this very reason, the knowledge of non-conceptual great bliss does not have all conceptual constructions as its cause. [End of] Karmamudrā.

However, by means of the two mudrās—the action seal (*karmamudrā*) and the knowledge seal (*jñānamudrā*)—only the skillful means of cultivation based on great passion (*mahārāga*) is demonstrated; they do not, however, possess the power to generate non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpajñāna*). That "syllable" (*akṣara*) is the non-conceptual gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), in which the four bodies have become a single unified mass. Is this of an increasing nature and thus subject to growth, or is it of a non-increasing nature? It does not cohere with either alternative. For if it were of an increasing nature, its further growth would be redundant.

However, since that which has an unincreased intrinsic nature lacks the capacity for such action, he stated the three verses beginning with "Of the increased... (vv. 94–96) to demonstrate that the very same objection is not an objection when based upon ultimate truth:

"There can be no increase of what is already increased, nor indeed any decrease of what is already diminished. There is no setting of what has already set, nor any rising of what has already risen. (94)
There would be no burning of what is already burning, nor the covering of what is already covered;
there would be no birth for what is already born, and no death for what is already dead. (95)
For one who is liberated, there is no liberation; likewise, for one who does not abide, there is no abiding.
There is no coming-into-being for that which has not been, nor is there the continued existence of that which has already come into being.
There is no perishing of that which is imperishable, nor is there non-perishing of that which is imperishable.
If this is so, how could there be arising and cessation? To this he says "svabhāva... and so forth:
For phenomena that lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva), there is the illusory arising and likewise the destruction of illusion. (97)

Those phenomena which lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva) should be understood as having arising and cessation like an illusion. Thus, by means of the examples of illusion and so forth, everything is unceasing within conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya). He speaks of the refutation of adherence to the one-sided positions of existence and non-existence regarding the world—which is neither arisen nor ceased—in the following: "There is no destruction," and so forth: The elements do not undergo destruction; they are not born by way of intrinsic nature. This entire world is devoid of intrinsic nature, characterized solely by existence and non-existence. (98)

"Having existence and non-existence as its single characteristic" means that all-encompassing existence is non-existence, which is the manifestation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). That which has a single, undivided characteristic—that is, a single intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*)—consisting of those two, is so described. Thus it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna:
"The emptiness of an entity is not other than the entity; nor does non-existence exist apart from it.
Therefore, you have revealed that entities born of conditions are empty. (Catuḥstava 3.43)
The mind, embraced by its own wisdom, has entered the lotus at the vajra-jewel;
there, the movement residing in the moon is the meditation on the motionless syllable. (90)
The cultivation of body, speech, and mind occurs within the channels of body, speech, and mind;
the integration of the three vajras is the cultivation of gnosis within the Śaṅkhinī. (100)
And for those drops (bindu) melted by the passion of wisdom, which have entered the state of fullness from the head in succession, there is bondage in the ultimate sense. (101)

Just as the moon, as described, reaches fullness through its digits in due order, so too, when the latent impressions are removed, it becomes full; for this [enlightened state], there is neither diminution nor filling.
Thus, the knowledge arisen in sequence shall reach fullness through the stages (*bhūmi*).
In the extraction of the afflictions and so forth, it is already full; for it there is neither cutting away nor filling. (103)
Just as the moon at its midpoint is not stable even on the full-moon night, so too the mind, characterized by the latent tendencies of saṃsāra, is not stable in the immutable bliss. 104.
The two sides of arising and waning are established as the white and the black;
but that which is full, situated between them, is not established in the full.
When the mind is in the vajra-jewel, it becomes motionless at the moment of perfect awakening; that [mind] then fulfills all moments. 106.
There is no abiding for it in the bright fortnight, nor is there any going in the dark;
situated in the middle of both fortnights, it has reached the non-dual state in the full moon.
Its arising occurs from the uṣṇīṣa, and it becomes full at the vajramaṇi;
through passionlessness there is a loss of digits, and through the emission from the vajra there is fullness. (108)
Again there is rising in the *uṣṇīṣa*, and again fullness in the *maṇi*; through the absence of passion, there is a loss of digits, but no loss of gnosis for embodied beings. (109)
His nature of great bliss is expressed by the word "full" (pūrṇa);
he is the creator of all other states of being, both in their emanation and their withdrawal. || 110 ||
Just as the moon [is perceived] by its two phases and the sun likewise by its two solstices, so for you, nirvāṇa would arise and from that, existence (bhava) would arise again. 111.

When this [breath] is motionless during the full [state], there is complete fulfillment through the stages (*bhūmi*), by means of twenty-eight hundred breaths consumed within the moments of the imperishable (*akṣara*). (112)
Free from the two extremes, yet complete with the stages;
the meaning of truth in twelve aspects, the imperishable in sixteen aspects. (113)
The mind, filled with the stages, is the supreme non-duality; filled with the digits, it is the imperishable in sixteen forms. (114)
The mind is of a single meaning, non-dual in nature, the ultimate reality, and indestructible; having reached the state of fullness, it is completely perfect in every respect. || 115 ||
The great passion beginning with dispassion is the body-vajra, the great imperishable;
it is completely full of the latencies of both sides and is untainted. 116.

"One's own wisdom" (*svaprajñā*) is a statement referring to the dependence upon the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*), and the great seal (*mahāmudrā*). In that context, the "vibration" (*spanda*) is the clear fluid of the *bodhicitta*-drop located at the tip of the *vajra*, which arises from the meditation on the imagined action-seal and knowledge-seal; through the meditation on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), that very vibration becomes non-vibrating (*niḥspanda*). By the words beginning with "body" (*kāya*), etc., the purification of the individual meditations on the body and so forth within the channels (*nāḍī*) that are their respective supports is shown.

Furthermore, when the cultivation of innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*) occurs in the *śaṅkhinī*, then at that very moment the body and the other vajras shall become merged into a single unity with the innate. "From the head" means from the forehead. "The stage of fullness" (*pūrṇāpada*) means the secret lotus. "Binding" (*bandhana*) means the state of stabilization. "In the ultimate sense" (*paramārthata*) means through the cultivation of the reality of Mahāmudrā. That which is called "fullness" (*pūrṇā*) is the sixteenth digit, characterized by innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
That [first moment] fulfills all-knowledge because even the subsequent moments possess the same single nature as that first, non-conceptual, innate moment. And so it has been said:
"By whom one entity is seen in its true reality, by him all entities are seen in their true reality. (Cf. *Catuḥśataka* VIII.16).

Here, a *kṣaṇa* is characterized by an inhalation and exhalation (*śvāsocchvāsa*). It is numbered at twenty-one thousand six hundred, and is denoted by the term "all *kṣaṇas*. Among these, when eighteen hundred breaths are restrained—having become of a single essence with the signless, innate gnosis (*animitta-sahaja-jñāna*)—there is the attainment of the first stage (*bhūmi*). In this way, through the successive attainment of the twelve stages, there is the fulfillment of all *kṣaṇas*. "Of this" refers to that innate gnosis whose nature is the sixteenth digit (*kalā*).

"The loss of the digits" (*kalāhāni*) refers to the abandonment of only the fifteen digits, but not of the sixteenth digit; for that [sixteenth digit] departs only at the time of death. "Of the loss" (*hāneḥ*) refers to the element of passion (*rajodhātu*). "There is no loss of gnosis" (*jñānahānir na*) means there is no abandonment of the sixteenth digit. "Of this" (*asya*) refers to the gnosis whose nature is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). "The other state" (*anyabhāvāntaram*) is characterized by the presence and absence of the states of passion, dispassion, white, and black. "The two fortnights" (*pakṣadvayam*) refers to passion, dispassion, and so forth.

Regarding the entry into the gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukhajñāna*), he speaks of the state of being of one taste with the co-emergent (*sahaja*) in all phenomena by means of such similes as that of river water:
"Just as river water that has entered the ocean becomes equal to it."
In this way, this collection of entities would become equal to that imperishable. || 117 ||
Just as this collection of elements, when consumed, attains the state of taste, and seeds attain the nature of seeds at the time of fruition, free from the person (pudgala). (118)
In this way, even the aggregate of existents, when consumed by the supreme syllable,
attains the state of the supreme syllable while assuming the nature of all forms.

Just as a yogi who has first begun his practice, having arisen from a meditation realized through non-conceptual self-awareness, says, "This happiness was mine," it is not so for the yogi who has attained the state of perfection, because that state consists of bliss in every aspect. To demonstrate this very point, he states the analogy and its application with the verse beginning with *na daṃśa*: "When the poison has reached its full state, the bitten person does not feel pain at the site of the bite, nor anywhere else; likewise, one does not perceive objects through the doors of the senses when the poison has reached its full state. (120)
Thus, when the full digit has entered the mind, the yogi perceives true bliss neither in the jewel nor elsewhere, nor does he perceive sense objects through the doors of the senses. (121)

In that context, "the state of fullness" refers to the location of the *uṣṇīṣa*. "Mind" (*citta*) refers to the non-conceptual *bodhicitta*. "The full digit" (*pūrṇakalā*) refers to the attainment of the complete sixteen digits through the various stages, beginning with the natural outflow (*niḥsyanda*). With the analogy of mercury (*rasa*), he explains—via the two verses beginning with "Just as" (verses 122–123)—the skillful means of cultivating the *karmamudrā* for the sake of bringing to perfection the wisdom arisen from the non-conceptual *mahāmudrā*:
"Just as even a single portion of mercury, when situated within iron..."
One should pierce the iron, heated by a fierce fire, on all sides.
In the very same way, even when situated in a single location, the blissful and imperishable mind—though tormented by the fire of desire—pierces [all things] on every side. 123.
Just as there is no stain whatsoever in pierced metals,
so too there is no latent impression whatsoever in pierced minds.
For iron, having reached the state of being heated by fire, becomes stainless;
in the same way, the mind becomes increasingly stainless through the fire of passion. 125.
Just as a stone attains a state of blazing radiance through contact with a great jewel, so indeed does the mind attain a state of bliss through contact with the bliss of the immutable. 126.

Just as people are unable to ascertain the capacity of even a conventional mercury (*rasa*) to transmute iron and other metals, how much less could they do so for knowledge that possesses infinite ultimate qualities? Therefore, he says: "What is the point here," and so forth.
What is the use of saying much more in this regard from the perspective of worldly conventional truth (*lokasaṃvṛtisatya*)?
The true nature of the essence of iron cannot be conceptualized with respect to its capacity for penetration.
Is the existence of gnosis (*jñāna*) merely a conceptual construct (*vitarkya*), or does it exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*)?
It is for the purpose of piercing through the mind that is defiled by adventitious stains. (128)

In order to demonstrate that the perfuming (*adhivāsanā*) by the form of impurity (*mala*) is not established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), he presents four propositions with the verse beginning "not adventitious" (*nāgantuka*) [129], and establishes those very points with the two verses beginning "if" (*yadi*) [130–131]. To dispel the doubt—namely, whether, due to the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of cognition, there might be either annihilation (*uccheda*) or its nature as permanence (*śāśvatatā*)—he speaks of its marvelous nature through the distinction between the example and the illustrated by means of the two verses beginning "just as copper" (*tāmra*) [132–133]:
"Impurity is not adventitious in the mind, nor has it existed in the mind for a long time."
It is not born apart from the mind, nor does that imperishable one abide within the mind. || 129 ||
If the mind were originally pure and [the defilement] were merely adventitious, then from where could that [defilement], which has existed for a long time, have arisen from that very mind? (130)
If it were born without the mind, then it would be like a flower in the sky;
if it were always present within the mind, then it could never perish in any way. (131)
Just as the blackness of copper is destroyed by the application of mercury, yet its essential nature—which exists through its purity—is not destroyed; so it is here. (132)
In the same way, the impurity of the mind perishes through union with emptiness; yet its nature as gnosis, which abides in a state of purity, does not perish. (133)
Just as iron pierced by mercury does not return to the state of being ordinary iron, so too the mind pierced by happiness does not return to the state of suffering. || 134 ||

This is the intended meaning: Is that blackness (*kālimā*) non-different or different from the copper? If it were non-different, then through the application of mercury (*rasa*), upon the destruction of the blackness, there would also be the destruction of the copper, because [the two] are of the same nature. If, on the other hand, it were different, what would happen to the copper? [Nothing at all], because there would be no connection between them. Consequently, just as gold manifests in an inconceivable way through the removal of the blackness—which cannot be described as either different or non-different—[so too does the nature of gold appear].

In that very way, through the yoga of emptiness, by the removal of the stains of cognition, there arises non-conceptual knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñāna*), which is like a dream, the abode of an infinite multitude of qualities, and non-abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa. And so says the venerable Saraha:
"Due to the destruction of conceptual construction (*kalpa*), the foolish imagine the destruction of the intellect."
But from this very [work], there arises for the wise something indescribable that surpasses even the sky.
There is no sin greater than passion, and no merit greater than bliss;
therefore, O King, one should always cause the mind to enter into immutable bliss. 135.
The bliss of a young maiden cannot be described without sexual union;
having attained sexual union in her youth, she knows great happiness by herself. (136)
Thus, it cannot be described as happiness by those devoid of meditative concentration;
having attained the imperishable within concentration, one knows great bliss by oneself. (137)
Even by the omniscient ones, the knowledge of the bliss born of the syllable is regarded with apprehension;
likewise, detachment from the mind’s lack of bliss should never be cultivated. (138)

"Imperishable bliss" (*akṣarasukha*) refers to non-conceptual great bliss (*nirvikalpa-mahāsukha*). "Detachment" (*virāga*) refers to the attachment to death, which is the latent tendency (*vāsanā*) for passion within cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). "It should not be performed" (*na kartavya*) means it is not to be practiced. Why? Because the increase of cyclic existence has its root in the latent tendency for passion and in death. Therefore, he says "from death," and so forth: From death arises detachment; from detachment, the arising of suffering; from suffering, the exhaustion of the elements (*dhātu*) for men; and from that exhaustion, death is traditionally known to occur. (139)
For them, death is followed by rebirth, and from existence comes death and again the fall;
thus, for sentient beings, existence arises from the production of detachment, and not otherwise. (140)
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid the passion of emission, by which the yogi attains immutable bliss and liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra. || 141 ||
Even by people seeking happiness, the desire for the pleasure of death is not to be coveted; how then could it be desired by a yogi of reality? To this he says, "The lustful one," and so forth:
"Even a lustful man, through detachment, does not seek the treatises on love; how much less would a yogi, when my Tantra has been spoken, seek out suffering? (142)

Therefore, the unconstructed supreme immutable great bliss must be accomplished precisely through the yoga of the immutable non-conceptual bodhicitta, and not through the yoga of constructed syllables such as *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*. Hence, he says "semen," and so forth.
One should accomplish the supreme syllable by means of the nature of the immutable seminal essence (śukra).
When the support (ādhāra) undergoes emission, there is detachment (virāgatā) of that which is supported (ādheya). || 143 ||

As long as the relationship between the support and the supported has not reached the state of the imperishable, the mind that has attained the state of the imperishable is no longer characterized by the distinction of support and supported. 144.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even the conceptualization of a support and that which is supported does not exist. Therefore, he says "the mind" (*citta*) and so forth. For this very reason, clarifying the negation of the reality produced from imagined seed-syllables such as *hūṃ* for the body of the Blessed One—which has arisen from non-conceptual, syllable-less gnosis—he says "syllable" (*akṣara*) and so forth:
"But for the body arisen from syllables, which resides in the *ūrṇā*-wheel, O King, the union of *āli* and *kāli* is not accepted as the syllable *hūṃ*. (145)

Now, he explains the causal relationship between the non-conceptual, non-dual gnosis and its result from the perspective of conventional reality, beginning with the words "The image" (bimba) and so forth:
"The image arising from emptiness is the cause; the result is the bliss born of the immutable.
The cause is sealed by the result; the result is sealed by the cause. (146)
Holding the image of emptiness is the cause; holding the syllable of compassion is the fruit.
That which is inseparable from emptiness and compassion is the bodhicitta, the immutable. 147.

The form possessing all aspects arises from the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). "Born from the syllable" (*akṣaraja*) means born from the non-conceptual gnosis of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) in all its aspects. He clarifies the very meaning stated previously by the words beginning with "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) through another designation. By the words beginning with "devoid of nirvāṇa" (*nirvāṇarahita*), he dispels the doubt regarding the annihilation (*uccheda*) or permanence (*śāśvata*) of the reflection of emptiness and the gnosis of the syllable.
The reflection is devoid of nirvāṇa; the syllable transcends saṃsāra. Their union, free from permanence and annihilation, is the non-dual supreme [reality]. (148)
Anticipating the question of how the faults of nihilism and eternalism might be avoided, he says "non-existence" and so forth:
There is no non-existence of the reflection, because its characteristic is arising from non-existence;
there is no existence even of the syllable, because its characteristic is being produced from existence. (149)

In that regard, "because of the characteristic of arising from non-existence" means that there is the manifestation of that which is to be personally realized by yogins, which has arisen from the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and possesses all aspects. "Because of the characteristic of arising from existence" means that all aspects have arisen without being produced from the very beginning. For this very reason, he says "existence," and so forth:
"The union of existence and non-existence is the Vajrayoga, the other non-dual."
It is liberated from both form and formlessness, like a reflection in a mirror. || 150 ||
