The reflection does not enter into existence, nor does it enter into the imperishable nirvāṇa;
embraced by one another, it is the peaceful, supreme state of the neuter. 151.

"Free from form and formlessness" (rūpārūpavinirmukta) means being devoid of the grasping at permanence, annihilation, existence, non-existence, and so forth. Now, he explains the nature of non-duality through the absence of superimposition regarding the previously mentioned cause and effect:
"Because the cause, wisdom, is unborn, the fruit arises from the cause, wisdom.
Because the cause, wisdom, is unborn, that which is born of wisdom is not born of a cause. (152)

Therefore, the unsurpassed knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*) is not born of causes. Here, "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects. "From a cause" means from that which is characterized as existent, non-existent, both, or neither. "The fruit" is Buddhahood, consisting of non-referential compassion, which acts for the benefit of the world. And so it is said in the *Pañcalakṣābhidhānahevajra*: [152] Wisdom is emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects. "From a cause" means from that which has the characteristics of being existent, non-existent, both, or neither. "The fruit" is Buddhahood, whose nature is non-referential compassion, performing the welfare of the world. Thus, in the *Pañcalakṣahevajra*:
"Emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects is the cause from the beginning;
subsequently, non-referential compassion is the fruit that accomplishes the welfare of the world.

Thus, since the cause lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the fruit also is not born from a cause. If cause and fruit existed, there would be the relationship of the seal and the sealing; but when both of those lack intrinsic nature, how could that be? To this he says: "By the fruit," and so forth.
There is no mutual sealing by means of fruit and cause between one another. || 153 ||
Is it then the case that the relationship of cause and effect does not exist at all? To this, he says: "The cause," and so forth.
Whatever is a cause or an effect, all that is dependently originated; it is a reflection sealed by mutual dependence, neither arisen nor ceased. (154)
Wisdom is utterly extinguished, and the supreme imperishable has arisen;
it is the liberation from cause and fruit, not a mutual sealing.

This is the meaning: the causal relationship characterized by dependent origination, established through examples such as an illusion, exists indeed from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Therefore, the gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), which consists of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*) in the form of their union (*yuganaddha*) and is devoid of conceptualizations such as cause and effect, must be perpetually arisen. This very point is stated with the words beginning "mutually" (*anyonya*) [154b]. Thus, the venerable Saraha said: *Q/R Saraha; also Vyaktabhāvānugatatattvasiddhi 1! cited in Nāropā ad 103*
Victory to the one King of Bliss, who is without cause and eternally arisen for the worlds;
at the time of whose proclamation even the Omniscient One became impoverished of words.

If, first of all, phenomena are indeed neither born nor ceased, then how could the establishment of conventional discourse through the forms of the object of knowledge and its cognition occur? To that end, he says: "That [is] of one's own mind," and so forth: "The perception of an object of knowledge here, which is unborn and unceased, is that of one's own mind and not of anything else, because of the distinction from an external object of knowledge. (156)

The appearance of the knowable is like a dream, being by its very nature unarisen. How then can the Vijñānavādin maintain that consciousness is an ultimately real entity? Refuting this, he says: "Therefore, it is not possible for anything to stamp itself by itself anywhere. Does a great sword ever cut itself with its own blade? (157)
He provides an illustration by means of the form of the gnosis of great bliss produced from the image in all its aspects, which is non-conceptual: "Like a barren woman," and so forth.
"Just as pleasure might arise in a dream through union with the daughter of a barren woman, so it is for oneself through the service of the image arisen from space. (158)

This is the intended meaning: just as a sentient being, during the time of a dream, experiences pleasure through attachment to the daughter of a barren woman who is by her very nature unarisen, so too does the yogi of reality experience the non-conceptual great bliss (*mahāsukha*) which is undifferentiated from the image in all its aspects—[an image] that is by nature unarisen and has become one with it, and which is beyond conceptual construction. Now, regarding the statement "it is not wisdom," he describes the specific qualities of that non-conceptual great bliss-knowledge:
"It is neither wisdom nor is it means; it is the innate (*sahaja*), together with wisdom.
It is completely full of bliss and devoid of all obscurations. (159)
Like space, it is unobstructed, devoid of objects and sense organs;
it abides everywhere within all beings, indivisible and free from fragmentation. || 16o ||

Regarding the primordial wisdom of great bliss (*mahāsukhajñāna*)—which has reached the ultimate limit, is described in other tantras, and is designated by various names according to the intentions of sentient beings—the term "Self-Arisen" (*svayambhū*) is presented through three verses [162–163]. Immediately after the introductory statement, the explanation begins with the words "The Vajra is indivisible" [164], etc.:
"He is the Self-Arisen One, Vajrasattva, the one of great purpose, the supreme syllable."
Great passion, the Great Being, who brings delight to all sentient beings. || 161 ||
The Bodhisattva is great hatred, the destroyer of afflictions, the great enemy;
he is the Samayasattva, great delusion, who destroys the delusion of the dull-witted. || 162 ||
The Vajrayoga is the great wrathful one, the great enemy of the enraged Māras;
he is Kālacakra, the great greed who destroys the craving for the perishable. || 163 ||
The Blessed One has stated here that "vajra" means indivisible and possesses great significance;
the oneness of the three realms of existence is called "sattva," and that is said to be the supreme syllable.
Filled with the supreme unchanging bliss, perfected by the stages [of the path], he is the Great Passion, the Great Being, who brings joy to all sentient beings. || 165 ||
A being established in awakening is therefore a Bodhisattva, immovable;
he is the great hatred and the great enemy against the hosts of hatred such as the afflictions. || 166 ||
The pledge (*samaya*) is the moon, the nectar, the semen; its consumption is non-emission.
By this method, the pledge-being (*samayasattva*) is the destroyer of the delusion of the dull-witted. (167)
The oneness of all vajras with the syllables of the body of wisdom;
the great wrathful one, the great enemy of the Māras who take the form of anger. (168)
Through the means of great immutable bliss, one should never abandon the welfare of sentient beings;
having liberated sentient beings, he is free from great greed, being the destroyer of the craving for the mutable. 169.
For these six aspects thus described—the sensations of the knowledge of the syllables, as well as consciousness, form, mental formations, and perception—are the families of the aggregates. 170.
Fire, space, earth, wind, and water, in their respective order;
likewise, the mind, the eye, the ear, the body, the nose, and the tongue. (171)
Consisting of sound, taste, the dharma-element, smell, touch, and form, the King of Wrath, the six-faced and terrifying one, is purified by the six families. || 172 ||

Herein is the collective meaning: it is stated that the form of Vajrasattva, Bodhisattva, Mahāsattva, and Samayasattva is purified by the vajras of non-conceptual gnosis, mind, speech, and body; it consists of the nature of the outflow (*niḥṣyanda*), maturation (*vipāka*), human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and purity (*vaimalya*); its essence is the innate, enjoyment, and emanation bodies; and it is completely pure through the four families. Within this very same four-family system, one should understand that there are various distinctions of the four-family vows (*saṃvara*) in other tantras.

Likewise, there is the six-family [mandala], which is purified by the elements of fire, space, earth, wind, and water through non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpajñāna*), and consists of the aggregates of consciousness, feeling, perception, mental formations, and form; it is completely purified of great envy, great passion, great hatred, great delusion, great anger, and great greed, and is purified by the six Tathāgatas—Vajrasattva, Ratnasambhava, Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Amoghasiddhi, and Amitābha. By means of these four families and six families, the entire *Yoga* and *Yoginī* Tantra is pervaded.
Thus, the distinction between the four families and the six families has been explained as one.
The body, the secret organ, and the mind are always the threefold maṇḍala;
from the three vajras of wisdom and means, the state of Vajrasattva arises. 173.
This is the means for attaining consecration, the means for the supreme unchanging;
it is conjoined with the families of the channels and has been spoken by the Moon according to the summary instruction. (174)
By the words beginning with "kāya," the threefold maṇḍala is taught. "Guhyendriya" refers to the Vāgvajra. "Candra" is an address.
Whatever merit has been gained by me through this commentary on the *Sekoddeśa*, [may it be for the benefit of all].
By writing this, people shall proceed to the state of Vajrasattva.
The *Sekoddeśa-ṭippaṇī* is completed. This work is the composition of the scholar Śrīdharānanda, son of a virtuous man.
